content: During focus group discussions facilitated by CEDEP, men who have sex with men (MSM) have shown increased confidence and capacity for activism. They have actively demanded access to tailored services, such as condom-compatible lubricants, and more comprehensive information to address their specific needs. As a result, there has been a noticeable increase in community members visiting health facilities to access these services. Health-care workers provide quantitative feedback through peer educators regarding referrals and service uptake. In Nigeria, many individuals from key populations experience self-stigma, which arises when they internalize societal myths and prejudices perpetuated by family, friends, health workers, and society at large. This self-stigma can lead to feelings of shame, loss of self-esteem, and even thoughts of self-harm or suicide. The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIER), established in 2006, was created to combat discrimination and marginalization of lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) individuals, particularly in accessing health services. One of TIER’s projects, the Integrated MARPs HIV Prevention Programme (IMHIPP), focuses on reducing the impact of HIV on MSM, their sexual partners, and dependents by providing prevention, care, and support services in a legally constrained environment. IMHIPP employs advocacy, communication, and capacity-building strategies to address the needs of the MSM community. Advocacy efforts with key stakeholders aim to improve understanding of the human rights and needs of MSM and their families. Social media and community outreach are used to disseminate HIV-related information and education to MSM and broader communities. Selected MSM are trained as peer educators and supporters to mentor others. To encourage service uptake, referrals are made to pre-screened, sensitive, and knowledgeable providers who understand the unique needs of MSM. For those uncomfortable seeking services alone, IMHIPP offers accompanied visits to health facilities. Additionally, IMHIPP-trained providers deliver palliative care to MSM with AIDS-related illnesses. Monthly field visits monitor the accuracy of prevention messages received by clients, and field data is validated through telephone calls to ensure clients understand at least three HIV prevention strategies. Over 50 volunteers have been trained as peer educators, and more than 5,000 MSM living with HIV have received information and services, including antiretroviral therapy (ART) and psychosocial support. An impact evaluation survey in 2013 revealed that 73% of MSM reached through IMHIPP services reported correct and consistent condom use, compared to 43% at the program’s inception in 2009. However, the passage of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act in 2013 has hindered information dissemination and community gatherings, leading to the temporary suspension of some IMHIPP activities and a reduction in the number of clients reached monthly. In the Philippines, the Cebu Plus Association created a youth wing called Re-You in response to the high prevalence of HIV among young people in Cebu. Re-You runs a mobile education program called Responsible Youth-on-the-Move, offering education and voluntary counseling and testing for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) to young key populations, primarily young MSM aged 15–24. Supported by Youth LEAD and the Robert Carr Civil Society Networks Fund, the program uses a mobile van to reach various locations and provide on-the-spot services. Outreach areas include cruising sites and other gathering places for young MSM, with services typically offered at night for better accessibility. Outreach staff, who are themselves young MSM, address cultural stigma and confidentiality concerns by securing referral agreements with HIV-proficient physicians and social workers at government clinics and other health-service providers. Re-You observed that many young MSM lack knowledge about available services, particularly for STI management, and some fear taking an HIV test due to concerns about coping with a positive diagnosis. The program builds trust by emphasizing the voluntary nature of testing and offering referrals to support services. In Russia, the MenZDRAV Foundation, in partnership with the NGO Phoenix PLUS, provides services to young MSM living with HIV, aged 18–25, across six regions. Due to fears of public identification of their sexual orientation or HIV status, many young men are reluctant to attend support groups. The Positive Life program offers individual counseling via phone, social media, and Skype. Peer counselors maintain telephone hotlines and provide information on sexuality, safe sex, STIs, ART adherence, and disclosure of HIV status to sexual partners. Those hesitant to visit the project office are referred to trained and sensitized medical specialists who provide stigma-free services. Since 2012, around 3,000 MSM living with HIV have received informational materials, and approximately 15,000 individuals regularly use the program’s website. In 2013, Positive Life counselors conducted nearly 1,900 phone consultations and 1,350 online consultations. In South Africa, the Health4Men project addresses the diverse sexual health needs of men, particularly vulnerable and marginalized groups like MSM. The project aims to institutionalize competence in serving the MSM community within existing public clinics. This involves sensitization to change attitudes, medical training to expand knowledge, mentoring to translate knowledge into skills, and ongoing technical support. Health4Men has developed two Centers of Excellence for MSM in Cape Town and Johannesburg, supported by satellite clinics. These clinics provide services for the MSM community, while outreach activities stimulate demand for services. Since its inception, over 3,000 health workers have been trained, 584 clinicians mentored, and 64 clinics declared competent to serve MSM. By the end of 2015, over 160 sites nationally were expected to be competent in serving MSM. In Indonesia, the HIV Cooperation Programme for Indonesia (HCPI) provides comprehensive HIV prevention and harm reduction services for people who inject drugs. The program builds links with government health services to facilitate access to early HIV testing and treatment, basic health care, methadone maintenance treatment, needle and syringe programs, and sexual and reproductive health services. Activities are implemented through partnerships that leverage the strengths of community-based organizations and government structures.
